rv.q: The jokes are plentiful and well executed enough that if you don’t like one bit of wordplay or slapstick or song, there’s a fair chance you will like the next.
It’s fun enough, but you may want to save your shekels.
But the production’s anything-for-a-laugh approach means we miss the point that this play, like all great comedies, has a tragic undertow.
The evening has its moments but the whole thing might have been funnier if Mr Foley had trusted Moliere a little more.
The laughs come thick and fast through the ensuing chaos, and with some stand out comedic performances, it seems like there’s still plenty of life in Molière’s old Miser yet.
Such a production requires split-second timing and this production never falters (well, hardly ever).
Inevitably this will have massive appeal to a certain class of theatregoer, while repelling others.
This may not be 1668 very exactly, but it's the nearest to one side of Moliere we've seen for years, and conveys something of the shock of his new.
Not that anyone would know it from seeing Sean Foley’s current production, which makes TV’s ’Allo ’Allo look like Chekhov.

Every now and then a show which deserves to be left at the interval – especially given today's prices – comes along and this is such a show, a dazzling addition to the list of unforgettable productions to disgrace the West End.

cn.t: This free adaptation delivers frequent laughs and strong comic performances from Griff Rhys Jones and Lee Mack, but its anything-for-a-laugh approach divides critics—some enjoy the manic energy while others find it betrays Molière's darker depths.
